scenario: AITA for adopting a puppy when we were notified the foster wanted to adopt the puppy, we were notified after a week of adotion process | My fiancee, her son (9), and I just moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. We have applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. After sending 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and being put on waitlists we finally got the call that we were set for an interview. We had initially been second in line but something from the first interview didn't work out so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did an interview the next day and everything went well and the adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet and greet. Tuesday afternoon we got a call from the agency that the medical went well and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically the foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency says they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. Have already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine year old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news we may not get her now. Am I the asshole if we adopted the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm "the asshole" in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. My fiancÃ©e, her son (who's 9 years old), and I just moved into a new house where we have no restrictions on owning a dog. That's great because we've been wanting to get a puppy for a while. We applied to adopt a puppy through a local rescue/adoption agency. We sent out 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and were put on waitlists. Finally, we got a call saying we were set for an interview. Initially, we were second in line, but something from the first interview didn't work out, so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did the interview the next day, and everything went well. The adoption coordinators said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday, we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet-and-greet. On Tuesday afternoon, we got a call from the agency that the medical went well, and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically, foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster, and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency said they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We've been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. We've already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine-year-old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news that we may not get her now. So, the question is: Am I the asshole if we adopt the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her? First, I need to understand the dynamics here. Foster homes usually have the first choice to adopt the animals they care for. That makes sense because they've been taking care of the puppy, bonding with it, and are familiar with its needs. It's a common practice in adoption processes to give foster families priority. However, in this case, the agency made a mistake by listing the puppy as available for adoption when it shouldn't have been. That's a significant error on their part. They should have known that the puppy was already with a foster family who had the first option to adopt. Now, we, as potential adopters, went through the process, got excited, bought supplies, and even told our friends and family about the puppy. Our son is particularly attached to the idea of getting this puppy, and he's heartbroken at the possibility of not getting her. On one hand, it's understandable that we're emotionally invested and want to proceed with the adoption. We've already taken steps and made plans based on the assumption that we would adopt this puppy. On the other hand, the foster family has a legitimate claim to the puppy, especially since the agency erred in listing the puppy as available. I'm also thinking about the emotional impact on our son. He's only nine, and being told that he might not get the puppy he's been looking forward to could be devastating. It's important to consider his feelings in this decision. But then, there's the issue of fairness to the foster family. They've been caring for the puppy, and it's their right to adopt if they choose to. The agency's mistake shouldn't take away their opportunity to keep the puppy they've bonded with. I'm also wondering about the policies of the adoption agency. Typically, foster homes have the first option, and if they choose not to adopt, then the puppy becomes available to the public. In this case, the agency mistakenly listed the puppy as available, which led to our application and the subsequent excitement. So, if we proceed with the adoption, are we taking advantage of the agency's mistake? Or are we within our rights to adopt the puppy since we went through the process and the foster family only expressed interest after we were already involved? It's a tricky situation. On one side, we have our emotional investment and the impact on our son. On the other side, we have the foster family's right to adopt the puppy they've been fostering. I think it's important to communicate openly with the foster family and the adoption agency. Maybe there's a way to resolve this that's fair to everyone involved. Perhaps the agency can facilitate a discussion between us and the foster family to find a mutually agreeable solution. In the end, the decision should balance our feelings with the rights and interests of the foster family. It's a tough call, but I believe that respecting the foster family's first choice is the right thing to do, even though it's disappointing for us and especially for our son.
